\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Execution Traces for Code LLMs}

Execution traces have been increasingly explored as supplementary signals for code language models, but existing work focuses almost exclusively on generation tasks such as code repair and synthesis.
\cite{placeholder_WangEMNLP2025} provide the most comprehensive study to date, showing that execution trace SFT yields limited improvements for code generation across multiple settings---a finding we complement by demonstrating that traces become highly effective when the downstream task shifts from generation to classification.
\cite{placeholder_NiICML2024} use self-training on execution traces as chain-of-thought rationales, improving MBPP fix rates by 26.1\%, while \cite{placeholder_JungEMNLP2025} extract step-by-step traces via the Python debugger Snoop to construct CoT supervision.
Both treat traces as intermediate reasoning scaffolds for producing code, leaving the question of trace utility for binary judgments entirely unexamined.

A parallel line of work investigates what trace content to retain.
\cite{placeholder_FerrandoArXiv2025} show that compact scratchpads recording only changed values match or exceed full-state scratchpads, providing early evidence that value-level information is largely redundant.
\cite{placeholder_DemystifyingArXiv2025} corroborate this from the model capability side, finding that LLMs are substantially weaker at value tracking than at structural understanding.
TraceCoder \cite{placeholder_TraceCoderICSE2026} demonstrates that selective variable probing outperforms full traces by 34.43\% on Pass@1, and TraceRepair \cite{placeholder_TraceRepairArXiv2026} uses critical variable snapshots to repair 392 defects.
ND-Slicer \cite{placeholder_YadavallyFSE2024} proposes execution-aware pretraining to learn dynamic dependencies, and \cite{placeholder_PredSlicingFSE2024} introduces assertion-point slicing conceptually close to our snapshot design.
\cite{placeholder_HaqueACL2025} observe that trace benefits diminish as program complexity increases, while ET-CoT \cite{placeholder_ETCoTICML2025} pushes granularity to the sub-line level on CRUXEval.

These compression strategies all optimize traces for generation fluency.
Our work departs from this paradigm: for a classification objective with $O(1)$ output entropy, the optimal representation is not a compressed execution narrative but a decision-relevant event summary---a principle that yields 99.2\% verdict accuracy where full traces reach only 81.8\%.

\subsection{Fine-Tuning LLMs for Classification}

Adapting generative LLMs to classification raises distinct design questions around input representation and training objective.
\cite{placeholder_YousefiArXiv2025} compare embedding-based and instruction-based SFT for text classification, finding task-dependent trade-offs between the two paradigms.
FisherSFT \cite{placeholder_FisherSFTICML2025} leverages Fisher information to select maximally informative training subsets, improving sample efficiency for classification fine-tuning.
\cite{placeholder_BucherArXiv2024} show that fine-tuned small models consistently outperform zero-shot GPT-4 on classification benchmarks, reinforcing that SFT remains the dominant approach for binary prediction tasks.

None of these studies consider structured program execution data as input, nor do they examine how input granularity interacts with classification accuracy.
Our work bridges this gap by treating the trace format itself as a first-class design variable: when the task is binary verdict prediction, the choice of trace abstraction has a larger effect on accuracy (+24.1 points) than the choice of whether to include traces at all (+6.7 points).

\subsection{Code Correctness Prediction}

Predicting whether code is correct constitutes the task most directly related to ours, yet prior approaches rely on static representations.
APPT \cite{placeholder_APPTTSE2024} combines BERT embeddings with LSTM sequence modeling for automated patch correctness classification, reaching 79.7\% accuracy---the closest prior baseline to our verdict task setting.
\cite{placeholder_SpiessICSE2025} show that code generation models are poorly calibrated when repurposed for correctness judgments, motivating dedicated classification architectures over repurposed generators.
At industry scale, \cite{placeholder_FosterFSE2025} build a mutation equivalence detector at Meta achieving 0.95 precision, demonstrating that binary code judgments can reach high reliability through domain-specific design.

No prior code correctness predictor incorporates execution traces as input.
VOTA closes this gap by pairing trace abstraction with verdict-specific compression: reducing full execution traces to exception-type events raises accuracy from 75.1\% (no trace) past 81.8\% (full trace) to 99.2\%, with the exception-only variant reaching 99.83\%---indicating that for pass/fail judgments, knowing \emph{what went wrong} matters far more than knowing \emph{what happened}.
